ap_physics_c_mechanics-f01.title: Uniform rod released from the horizontal

stimulus.description: A uniform rod of mass $M=1\text{ kg}$ and length $L=1\text{ m}$ is held horizontal and is free to rotate about a frictionless horizontal pivot at one end. The rotational inertia of the rod about the pivot is $\tfrac13ML^2$. The rod is released from rest. Use $g=9.8\text{ m/s}^2$.

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: On the dot below, which represents the center of mass of the rod at the instant of release, draw and label the forces (not components) that act on the rod. Each force must be represented by a distinct arrow starting on the dot.
parts.model_answer: Two arrows from the dot: the weight straight down and the force of the pivot straight up (its magnitude is less than the weight because the center of mass accelerates downward).

rubric_rows.criterion: Draws and labels the weight (down) and the force exerted by the pivot (up), with no extra force such as a force of rotation
common_errors: adds a force of rotation
draws only the weight

rubric_rows.criterion: The directions are correct: weight straight down and the pivot force straight up
common_errors: draws the pivot force horizontal at the instant of release

rubric_rows.criterion: The weight arrow is longer than the pivot-force arrow because the center of mass accelerates downward
common_errors: draws equal lengths for an accelerating rod

parts.label: B
parts.prompt: Derive an expression for the angular acceleration $\alpha$ of the rod just after the release in terms of $g$ and $L$.
parts.model_answer: The torque of the weight about the pivot is $Mg(L/2)$, so $\alpha=\tau/I=Mg(L/2)/(\tfrac13ML^2)=3g/(2L)$.

rubric_rows.criterion: Finds the torque of the weight about the pivot, $\tau=Mg(L/2)$, using the center of mass at $L/2$
common_errors: uses the lever arm L

rubric_rows.criterion: Applies $\tau=I\alpha$ with $I=\tfrac13ML^2$
common_errors: uses the rotational inertia about the center, $\tfrac1{12}ML^2$

rubric_rows.criterion: Obtains $\alpha=3g/(2L)$ (the mass cancels)
common_errors: obtains $g/L$

parts.label: C
parts.prompt: Calculate the angular speed of the rod when it is vertical, for $L=1\text{ m}$.
parts.model_answer: $Mg(L/2)=\tfrac12(\tfrac13ML^2)\omega^2$ gives $\omega=\sqrt{3g/L}\approx5.42\text{ rad/s}$.

rubric_rows.criterion: Equates the loss of gravitational energy of the center of mass to the rotational kinetic energy: $Mg(L/2)=\tfrac12I\omega^2$
common_errors: uses the drop L for the center of mass

rubric_rows.criterion: Obtains about 5.42 with units of radians per second

parts.label: D
parts.prompt: A second rod of the same length but twice the mass is released in the same way. Does the angular acceleration just after the release increase, decrease or stay the same? Justify your answer.
parts.model_answer: It stays the same, because the torque $Mg(L/2)$ and the rotational inertia $\tfrac13ML^2$ are both proportional to $M$ and the mass cancels in $\alpha=3g/(2L)$.

rubric_rows.criterion: States that the angular acceleration stays the same
common_errors: states that the angular acceleration doubles

rubric_rows.criterion: Justifies that the mass appears in both the torque and the rotational inertia and cancels in $\alpha=3g/(2L)$
common_errors: argues only that all objects fall at the same rate

The rotational inertia of the rod about the pivot is $\tfrac13ML^2$. The rod is released from rest. Use $g=9.8\text{ m/s}^2$.

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: On the dot below, which represents the center of mass of the rod at the instant of release, draw and label the forces (not components) that act on the rod. Each force must be represented by a distinct arrow starting on the dot.
parts.model_answer: Two arrows from the dot: the weight straight down and the force of the pivot straight up (its magnitude is less than the weight because the center of mass accelerates downward).

rubric_rows.criterion: Draws and labels the weight (down) and the force exerted by the pivot (up), with no extra force such as a force of rotation
common_errors: adds a force of rotation
draws only the weight

rubric_rows.criterion: The directions are correct: weight straight down and the pivot force straight up
common_errors: draws the pivot force horizontal at the instant of release

rubric_rows.criterion: The weight arrow is longer than the pivot-force arrow because the center of mass accelerates downward
common_errors: draws equal lengths for an accelerating rod

parts.label: B
parts.prompt: Derive an expression for the angular acceleration $\alpha$ of the rod just after the release in terms of $g$ and $L$.
parts.model_answer: The torque of the weight about the pivot is $Mg(L/2)$, so $\alpha=\tau/I=Mg(L/2)/(\tfrac13ML^2)=3g/(2L)$.

rubric_rows.criterion: Finds the torque of the weight about the pivot, $\tau=Mg(L/2)$, using the center of mass at $L/2$
common_errors: uses the lever arm L

rubric_rows.criterion: Applies $\tau=I\alpha$ with $I=\tfrac13ML^2$
common_errors: uses the rotational inertia about the center, $\tfrac1{12}ML^2$

rubric_rows.criterion: Obtains $\alpha=3g/(2L)$ (the mass cancels)
common_errors: obtains $g/L$

parts.label: C
parts.prompt: Calculate the angular speed of the rod when it is vertical, for $L=0.8\text{ m}$.
parts.model_answer: $Mg(L/2)=\tfrac12(\tfrac13ML^2)\omega^2$ gives $\omega=\sqrt{3g/L}\approx6.06\text{ rad/s}$.

rubric_rows.criterion: Equates the loss of gravitational energy of the center of mass to the rotational kinetic energy: $Mg(L/2)=\tfrac12I\omega^2$
common_errors: uses the drop L for the center of mass

rubric_rows.criterion: Obtains about 6.06 with units of radians per second

parts.label: D
parts.prompt: A second rod of the same length but twice the mass is released in the same way. Does the angular acceleration just after the release increase, decrease or stay the same? Justify your answer.
parts.model_answer: It stays the same, because the torque $Mg(L/2)$ and the rotational inertia $\tfrac13ML^2$ are both proportional to $M$ and the mass cancels in $\alpha=3g/(2L)$.

rubric_rows.criterion: States that the angular acceleration stays the same
common_errors: states that the angular acceleration doubles

rubric_rows.criterion: Justifies that the mass appears in both the torque and the rotational inertia and cancels in $\alpha=3g/(2L)$
common_errors: argues only that all objects fall at the same rate

ap_physics_c_mechanics-f02.title: Position and velocity graphs of a block on a spring

stimulus.description: A block of mass $m=1\text{ kg}$ is attached to a horizontal ideal spring of spring constant $k=40\text{ N/m}$ on a frictionless surface. The block is pulled to $x=+A$ with $A=0.2\text{ m}$ and released from rest at $t=0$. Blank axes are provided on the answer sheet.

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: On the axes provided, sketch the position $x$ and the velocity $v$ of the block as functions of time $t$ for one full period (use two separate sets of axes stacked vertically with the same time scale). Label the amplitudes and the period.
parts.model_answer: $x(t)$ is a cosine starting at $+0.2\text{ m}$ with period $T=0.99\text{ s}$; $v(t)$ is a negative sine, zero at $t=0$, reaching $-1.26\text{ m/s}$ at $T/4$.

rubric_rows.criterion: Both sets of axes are labeled with quantities and units and share the same time scale
The position graph is a cosine that starts at $+A=0.2\text{ m}$
common_errors: starts at zero like a sine

rubric_rows.criterion: The velocity graph is zero at $t=0$ and first becomes negative, reaching about $-1.26\text{ m/s}$ at a quarter period
common_errors: draws the velocity as a positive cosine

rubric_rows.criterion: The period is marked as about $0.99\text{ s}$ on the time axis
common_errors: marks half of the period

parts.label: B
parts.prompt: Derive an expression for the maximum speed of the block in terms of $A$, $k$ and $m$.
parts.model_answer: $x=A\cos\omega t$ with $\omega=\sqrt{k/m}$, so $v=dx/dt=-A\omega\sin\omega t$ and $v_{max}=A\sqrt{k/m}$.

rubric_rows.criterion: Identifies the angular frequency $\omega=\sqrt{k/m}$
common_errors: uses $\omega=\sqrt{m/k}$

rubric_rows.criterion: Differentiates the position function to find the velocity $v=-A\omega\sin\omega t$
required_elements: v = - A omega sin omega t
common_errors: differentiates cos to sin without the factor omega

rubric_rows.criterion: Obtains $v_{max}=A\sqrt{k/m}$
common_errors: omits the square root

parts.label: C
parts.prompt: Calculate the period, the maximum speed and the magnitude of the maximum acceleration of the block.
parts.model_answer: $T=2\pi\sqrt{m/k}\approx0.99\text{ s}$, $v_{max}=A\sqrt{k/m}\approx1.26\text{ m/s}$ and $a_{max}=A\omega^2=kA/m\approx8.00\text{ m/s}^2$.

rubric_rows.criterion: Calculates the period of about 0.99 with units of seconds
common_errors: omits the $2\pi$

rubric_rows.criterion: Calculates the maximum speed of about 1.26 with units of meters per second
common_errors: omits the square root

rubric_rows.criterion: Calculates the maximum acceleration of about 8.00 with units of meters per second squared
common_errors: uses $A\omega$ for the acceleration

parts.prompt: The block is replaced by one with four times the mass and released from the same position. Predict by what factors the period and the maximum speed change, and justify your answer.

common_errors: states a factor of 4 for the period

rubric_rows.criterion: Justifies with $T\propto\sqrt{m}$ and $v_{max}\propto1/\sqrt{m}$ (same stored energy shared with a larger mass)
common_errors: argues only that the heavier block is slower

ap_physics_c_mechanics-f03.title: Experiment: spring constant from the period of a hanging block

stimulus.description: A student hangs a block of mass m from a vertical spring of unknown spring constant k, pulls it down a small distance and releases it, and measures the period T of the oscillation for several masses.

notes: A student hangs a block of mass m from a vertical spring of unknown spring constant k, pulls it down a small distance and releases it, and measures the period T of the oscillation for several masses.

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: Describe an experimental procedure to collect the data for the period as a function of the mass. Include the equipment and the measurements, how the independent variable is changed, and one way to reduce the uncertainty in the measured period.
parts.model_answer: Measure each mass with a balance (or use known slotted masses); displace the block a small distance and time 10 oscillations with a stopwatch, dividing to find the period; change only the hanging mass with the same spring and the same small starting displacement; reduce the timing uncertainty by timing many oscillations or repeating the trials and averaging.

parts.model_answer: $m_1v=(m_1+m_2)v_f$ gives $v_f=m_1v/(m_1+m_2)=2.00\text{ m/s}$ and the lost fraction is $1-K_f/K_i=m_2/(m_1+m_2)=0.333$.

parts.label: C
parts.prompt: The stationary cart is replaced by one with twice the mass, $2\text{ kg}$. Does the fraction of the initial kinetic energy that is lost increase, decrease or stay the same? Give its new value and justify your answer.
parts.model_answer: It increases to $2m_2/(m_1+2m_2)=0.500$, because the lost fraction $m_2/(m_1+m_2)$ increases with $m_2$.

rubric_rows.criterion: States that the lost fraction increases to about 0.500
common_errors: states that the fraction is unchanged

rubric_rows.criterion: Justifies with $m_2/(m_1+m_2)$, which increases with $m_2$ (a heavier target makes the final speed smaller and the loss larger)
common_errors: argues only that heavier objects lose more energy
